articles.label: Infrastructure
articles.headline: Pensacola's $2.3M sidewalk gap: Why the same five corridors keep losing federal grants
articles.dek: City engineers have applied for Safe Streets funding three years running. Each time, the same stretches of Cervantes and Pace fail to score. Internal memos show why.
brief: Pensacola has submitted Safe Streets grant applications for the same five sidewalk corridors since 2024, requesting a total of $2.3 million, and has been rejected each time
Internal city memos obtained through public records requests reveal scoring deficiencies tied to incomplete crash data, missing ADA transition plans, and lack of documented community engagement
City engineers say they lack the staff and budget to fix the application problems, while pedestrian advocates point to three fatalities on the unfunded corridors since 2023
articles.body:
The crosswalk at Cervantes Street and N Street has no curb ramps. The asphalt crumbles where sidewalk should be. A faded memorial cross leans against a utility pole twenty feet from the intersection, plastic flowers bleached by two summers of Gulf Coast sun.

This stretch of Cervantes, from Palafox to 17th Avenue, appears on every Safe Streets and Roads for All grant application Pensacola has submitted since the federal program launched. So does the western segment of Pace Boulevard between Fairfield Drive and Jackson Street. So do three other corridors totaling 4.2 miles of missing or substandard sidewalk.

Three applications. Three rejections. $2.3 million requested and never received.

Internal memos obtained by The Flightline through public records requests show the city knows exactly why it keeps losing. The applications score poorly on the same metrics year after year: incomplete crash data, missing ADA transition plans, and insufficient documentation of community input.

City engineers say they don't have the resources to fix the problems. Pedestrian advocates say the city isn't trying hard enough. Three people have died on the unfunded corridors since 2023.

The scoring problem

The Safe Streets and Roads for All program, administered by the U.S. Department of Transportation, awards grants to local governments for pedestrian and cyclist safety improvements. Applications are scored on a 100-point scale. Projects must clear 70 points to advance to funding consideration.

Pensacola's 2024 application scored 58. The 2025 application scored 61. This year's application, submitted in February, scored 64.

Progress. But not enough.

A March 2026 memo from Public Works Director Sandra Okafor to City Administrator Keith Wilkins breaks down where the points are lost. Crash data documentation accounts for 15 possible points. Pensacola has claimed between 6 and 8 in each application cycle.

"Our crash data comes from FDOT's Signal Four Analytics system," Okafor wrote. "The federal reviewers want localized data that shows specific corridor conditions over a five-year period. We don't maintain that level of granularity internally."

The Escambia County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol report crashes to the state system. The city has no independent crash database for its roads. Extracting corridor-specific data requires manual review of individual reports.

"We estimated 40 staff hours to compile compliant data for all five corridors," Okafor wrote. "We do not have 40 hours."

The ADA gap

Federal applications also require documentation of ADA compliance planning. Pensacola's ADA transition plan dates to 2012. It has not been updated.

ADA transition plans identify barriers to accessibility in public infrastructure and establish timelines for correction. The 2012 plan identified 847 non-compliant curb ramps citywide. As of April 2026, city records show 312 have been replaced or upgraded.

The remaining 535 represent a compliance rate of 37 percent over 14 years.

"Reviewers look for active planning, not legacy documents," Okafor's memo states. "Our 2012 plan shows progress but does not meet current federal expectations for a comprehensive, updated assessment."

Updating the plan would require a new citywide survey. Public Works has not budgeted for one. Okafor estimated the cost at $180,000 to $240,000 for a consultant-led assessment.

The community input question

Grant applications must demonstrate community engagement. Pensacola's submissions have cited two public meetings held in 2023 as part of the city's broader transportation master plan process.

Those meetings covered all transportation issues citywide. Attendance records show 34 residents at one, 41 at the other. The applications do not include corridor-specific outreach for Cervantes, Pace, or the three other target areas.

"We haven't done dedicated engagement for these projects because the projects don't exist yet," said Michael Reyes, the city's transportation planner. "You don't usually do community meetings for grant applications. You do them when you have money to build something."

Federal reviewers see it differently. The scoring rubric awards points for "demonstrated community support and input specific to proposed project areas." Pensacola has received between 4 and 6 points out of a possible 12 in this category.

The human cost

Carmen Delgado's son Julio was killed on Pace Boulevard in October 2024. He was walking home from his job at a Waffle House near Fairfield Drive. No sidewalk. No crosswalk. A driver struck him at 9:47 p.m.

Delgado attended a Pensacola City Council meeting in January 2025 to ask about sidewalk improvements on Pace. She was told the city had applied for federal funding.

"They said they were working on it," Delgado said. "That was a year and a half ago. Nothing's different. People still walk in the road."

Two other pedestrian fatalities have occurred on the five corridors since the city began applying for Safe Streets funding. Walter Simmons, 67, was struck on Cervantes near A Street in March 2023. Keisha Morrow, 29, died on Pace Boulevard south of Brent Lane in August 2025.

All three deaths occurred in areas with missing sidewalks or non-compliant crossings.

What it would cost to fix

The city's $2.3 million ask would not complete all five corridors. It would fund approximately 2.8 miles of new sidewalk construction and 47 ADA-compliant curb ramp installations.

Full buildout of pedestrian infrastructure on all five corridors would cost an estimated $6.1 million, according to a 2024 engineering assessment commissioned by Public Works.

Pensacola's annual capital improvement budget allocates approximately $400,000 to sidewalk projects. At that rate, completing the five corridors without federal help would take more than 15 years.

"We're not choosing not to fix this," Reyes said. "We're choosing between this and a dozen other things the city needs. Stormwater. Roads. Parks. There's only so much money."

What other cities do

Tallahassee received $4.2 million in Safe Streets funding in 2025 for pedestrian improvements near Florida State University. Its application scored 81 points.

Jacksonville received $7.8 million for sidewalk gaps on the Westside. It scored 77.

Both cities have dedicated grant writers on staff. Both updated their ADA transition plans within the past three years. Both conducted corridor-specific community engagement before applying.

Pensacola has one part-time grant coordinator who handles applications across all city departments.

"The cities that win these grants invest in winning them," said Patricia Underwood, executive director of Walk Pensacola, a pedestrian advocacy nonprofit. "Pensacola keeps submitting the same application with the same holes and expecting a different result."

The path forward

Okafor's memo to Wilkins concludes with three recommendations: hire a dedicated transportation grant writer, contract for an updated ADA transition plan, and conduct corridor-specific community meetings before the 2027 application cycle.

Total estimated cost: $320,000 to $380,000.

The memo does not identify a funding source for these investments. City Council has not discussed the recommendations in any public meeting. Wilkins did not respond to requests for comment.

The 2027 Safe Streets application deadline is February 15. If Pensacola applies again with the same documentation, city engineers expect a score in the mid-60s.

Not enough.

The memorial cross at Cervantes and N Street has been there since 2019. No one at City Hall could say whose name is on it. The plastic flowers were replaced sometime last fall.

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: The 400 short-term rentals Pensacola Beach doesn't count
articles.dek: Santa Rosa Island Authority tracks licensed vacation rentals. It doesn't track the ones operating without permits. A Flightline analysis of booking platforms found a shadow market thriving in plain sight.
brief: A Flightline analysis identified approximately 400 short-term rental listings on Pensacola Beach that do not appear in Santa Rosa Island Authority permit records
Unlicensed operators avoid SRIA lease fees, potentially costing the authority hundreds of thousands in annual revenue
SRIA officials acknowledge enforcement gaps but say they lack resources for systematic monitoring of booking platforms
articles.body:
The listing promises everything a beach vacation should be. Three bedrooms, Gulf views, a private balcony. "Steps from the sand," the Airbnb page reads. "Your perfect Pensacola Beach getaway."

The property exists. The permit does not.

This unit on Via de Luna Drive is one of roughly 400 short-term rentals operating on Pensacola Beach without authorization from the Santa Rosa Island Authority, according to a Flightline analysis of major booking platforms conducted in April. The properties appear on Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com. They accept reservations. They collect fees. They do not appear in SRIA's licensing database.

The finding suggests a shadow vacation rental market generating millions in bookings annually while sidestepping the regulatory framework that governs the island's tourism economy.

What the numbers show

The Flightline compiled active rental listings from Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com for properties within SRIA's jurisdiction during the week of April 14-21. After removing duplicates across platforms and excluding listings that appeared to be long-term rentals, the analysis identified 1,847 distinct properties marketed for short-term stays.

SRIA's public licensing database lists 1,431 active short-term rental permits as of April 30.

The gap: 416 listings with no matching permit.

Some discrepancy is expected. Property names on booking platforms don't always match official records. A handful of listings may be newly permitted and not yet in the public database. Others might be errors—duplicate entries, properties just outside SRIA jurisdiction, or listings that are no longer active.

But even accounting for noise in the data, the scale suggests systematic non-compliance rather than isolated cases.

"Four hundred is not a rounding error," said Marcus Wellborn, a vacation rental consultant based in Destin who reviewed The Flightline's methodology. "That's a parallel market."

The cost of not counting

Pensacola Beach operates under a unique governance structure. The island is leased from Escambia County, and SRIA manages development through a system of subleases. Property owners don't own land outright—they hold long-term leases that come with annual fees.

Short-term rental operators pay additional fees on top of standard lease costs. A typical three-bedroom condo operating as a vacation rental pays roughly $1,200 annually in STR-specific fees, according to SRIA's fee schedule. That money funds beach maintenance, parking infrastructure and code enforcement.

If 400 properties are operating without permits, SRIA could be missing $480,000 or more in annual revenue. The actual figure depends on property sizes and rental volumes, but the order of magnitude is significant for an authority with a $14 million annual budget.

Then there's the tourism development tax. Escambia County collects a 5% tax on short-term rentals, revenue that funds Visit Pensacola and beach restoration projects. Licensed rental operators are registered to collect and remit the tax. Unlicensed ones may not be.

Escambia County Tax Collector's office declined to provide data on short-term rental tax compliance, citing ongoing reviews of collection procedures. A spokesperson said the office "relies on self-reporting and periodic audits" to ensure compliance.

Hiding in plain sight

The unlicensed rentals aren't hard to find. They advertise openly. They have reviews dating back years. They show up in search results alongside their permitted competitors.

One property on Avenida 23, listed on both Airbnb and Vrbo, has accumulated 47 reviews since 2022. It charges $275 per night in peak season. It does not appear in SRIA records under any variation of its listed address.

Another on Fort Pickens Road markets itself as "locally owned" and "family friendly." Its Airbnb profile shows availability through December. No permit on file.

The Flightline is not publishing specific addresses because property owners have not been given an opportunity to respond to individual findings. Some may have permits under different addresses or ownership structures. Others may have applied recently and not yet appeared in public records.

But the pattern suggests enforcement hasn't kept pace with the platform economy.

"The platforms made it too easy," said Carla Simmons, who manages six licensed vacation rentals on the beach for out-of-state owners. "You can have a listing up in twenty minutes. Nobody asks for your permit number until someone complains."

SRIA's response

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio acknowledged the authority does not systematically monitor booking platforms.

"We respond to complaints," Ghio said in an interview. "If someone reports an unlicensed rental, we investigate. But we don't have staff assigned to scraping Airbnb."

Ghio said SRIA receives between five and ten complaints about suspected unlicensed rentals annually. The authority investigates each one and has issued citations in some cases. But proactive enforcement would require additional staff or third-party services that aren't currently budgeted.

"It's a resource question," Ghio said. "We have four people in compliance. They're handling construction, signage, lease violations, everything. Adding short-term rental monitoring would mean taking them off something else."

Some Florida jurisdictions have contracted with companies like Granicus or Host Compliance to identify unlicensed rentals through automated platform monitoring. Santa Rosa Beach and Panama City Beach both use such services. SRIA has not.

When asked if the authority had considered these tools, Ghio said the board had "looked at proposals" but had not moved forward due to cost concerns. He declined to specify what vendors had proposed or what implementation would cost.

SRIA Board Chair Janet Pennington did not respond to requests for comment.

The platform question

Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com all have policies requiring hosts to comply with local regulations. All three platforms allow jurisdictions to require permit numbers in listings. Some cities have negotiated agreements requiring platforms to verify permits before listings go live.

SRIA has no such agreement.

Airbnb spokesperson Marcus Chen said the company "encourages hosts to understand and follow local rules" and provides resources about short-term rental regulations. He said Airbnb would "work with any jurisdiction interested in establishing a permit verification system."

Vrbo did not respond to requests for comment. Booking.com declined to discuss specific jurisdictions but said hosts "are responsible for ensuring their listings comply with applicable laws."

The absence of platform-level enforcement means the burden falls entirely on local authorities—authorities that, in SRIA's case, aren't equipped to carry it.

Who's affected

Licensed rental operators say the uneven playing field costs them bookings and undermines the fee structure they've agreed to support.

"I pay my SRIA fees, I pay my taxes, I carry the insurance they require," said Daniel Okonkwo, who owns two rental condos in the Portofino complex. "The guy down the hall is doing the same thing I'm doing, but he's not paying any of that. How is that fair?"

Okonkwo estimated his annual compliance costs—SRIA fees, business tax receipts, required insurance—run about $4,500 per unit. An unlicensed operator pockets that money as additional profit or uses it to undercut prices.

"They can afford to charge less because their costs are less," he said. "I'm competing with people who aren't playing by the same rules."

Condo association boards have also struggled with unauthorized rentals. Several Pensacola Beach HOAs have bylaws limiting or prohibiting short-term rentals, but enforcement depends on identifying violations—something the platforms make difficult.

"We find out when neighbors complain about noise or parking," said a board member at one beachfront complex who spoke on condition of anonymity to avoid conflict with unit owners. "By then they've been renting for months."

What happens next

Ghio said SRIA staff would "review" The Flightline's findings but could not commit to specific enforcement actions.

"If you're telling me there are four hundred unlicensed rentals out there, that's more than we can address with our current setup," he said. "We'd need board direction and probably a budget amendment to do anything systematic."

The next SRIA board meeting is scheduled for May 14. Short-term rental compliance is not currently on the agenda.

For now, the listings remain live. The bookings continue. And the gap between what's permitted and what's operating grows a little wider with each reservation.

The three-bedroom on Via de Luna has availability this weekend. Reviews call it "immaculate" and "perfectly located." The calendar shows it's booked solid through Memorial Day.

SRIA doesn't know it exists.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 150,000 visitors and one question: Where do they all park?
articles.dek: The July air show returns after last year's weather cancellation. Downtown merchants and base officials are still negotiating a shuttle plan that fell apart in 2024.
brief: The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show returns July 10-11 after Hurricane Claudette forced cancellation of the 2025 event
NAS Pensacola expects 150,000 visitors but has reduced on-base parking capacity by 40% due to ongoing runway construction
Downtown shuttle negotiations stalled after a 2024 pilot program left merchants complaining of lost revenue and blocked storefronts
articles.body:
The fence line along Blue Angel Parkway is already getting a fresh coat of white paint. Maintenance crews started Monday, working section by section toward the main gate at NAS Pensacola. By July, when 150,000 people descend on this stretch of road for the Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show, everything visible from the street will gleam.

What happens to all those people once they arrive is less certain.

The July 10-11 air show marks the first homecoming since 2024, after Hurricane Claudette's outer bands dumped six inches of rain on Pensacola last July and forced cancellation 48 hours before gates were scheduled to open. That storm cost the region an estimated $12 million in tourism revenue, according to Visit Pensacola figures. Hotels had been booked solid. Restaurants had staffed up. The planes never flew.

This year the weather is someone else's problem. The parking is not.

Fewer spaces, more people

Runway reconstruction at NAS Pensacola, a $47 million project that began in March 2025, has eliminated roughly 2,800 parking spaces that were available during previous homecoming events. The work zones and equipment staging areas now occupy what used to be overflow lots on the installation's north side.

"We're looking at approximately 4,200 on-base spaces available for the general public," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Dominguez, public affairs officer for NAS Pensacola, during an April 29 planning meeting at the Pensacola Bay Center. "That's down from about 7,000 in previous years."

The math doesn't work. At peak attendance, homecoming draws between 140,000 and 160,000 visitors across the two-day event. Even accounting for carpooling, military family access through separate gates, and VIP parking, the shortfall runs into the tens of thousands of vehicles.

The Navy's proposed solution: remote parking with shuttle service from downtown Pensacola and the Pensacola Bay Center lot.

Downtown merchants have heard this before.

The 2024 pilot that wasn't

In May 2024, NAS Pensacola and the Downtown Improvement Board announced a partnership to run shuttle buses from a staging area near the Wahoos stadium to the base's west gate. The plan promised to bring air show visitors within walking distance of Palafox Street restaurants and shops before and after the event.

Fourteen downtown business owners signed on. They agreed to adjusted hours and contributed to a $15,000 marketing fund promoting the shuttle route.

Then the details arrived.

The shuttle staging area would occupy 140 parking spaces on Chase Street for three days, including setup and breakdown. Buses would run every 15 minutes starting at 6 a.m. The route would block the intersections at Chase and Palafox for 30 to 45 seconds per bus cycle.

"We were told this would bring customers downtown," said Marcus Webb, owner of Palace Café on Palafox Street, at an October 2024 Downtown Improvement Board meeting. "What we got was our regular customers couldn't find parking and the shuttle people went straight to the base and straight back to their cars."

The hurricane made the dispute moot. The shuttle never ran. The marketing fund was partially refunded. The partnership dissolved without a formal postmortem.

New year, familiar arguments

Five months out from the 2026 show, the same parties are back at the table. NAS Pensacola needs the remote parking. Downtown merchants need assurances that their July weekend won't become a logistical sacrifice zone.

Pensacola City Council member Tenley Hughes, whose District 6 includes much of downtown, has attempted to broker a compromise. Her office proposed a three-part framework in late April: dedicated rideshare drop-off points at the base perimeter, a downtown shuttle route that avoids Palafox Street entirely, and a $50,000 city contribution to extend Escambia County Area Transit service hours during the event.

"The air show is a regional asset," Hughes said in an interview. "The parking problem is a regional problem. We can't solve it by making downtown absorb all the friction."

The Navy has not formally responded to Hughes' framework. Dominguez said discussions are ongoing and declined to comment on specific proposals.

Meanwhile, the Downtown Improvement Board has taken a harder line than in 2024. At its May 4 meeting, the board voted 7-2 to oppose any shuttle plan that stages buses within the core downtown grid bounded by Garden Street, Tarragona Street, Main Street, and the waterfront.

"We support the air show. We support the Navy. We do not support turning our streets into a bus depot," said DIB chair Carolyn Foster after the vote.

What 150,000 people look like

The scale of homecoming is difficult to convey without standing in it. At peak hours on Saturday afternoon, the crowd at Sherman Field resembles a football stadium that forgot to install seats. Families stake out patches of grass at dawn. The flight line becomes a river of people moving between static aircraft displays, food vendors, and the best sightlines for the demonstration.

Getting in is the easy part. Getting out can take three hours.

After the 2023 homecoming, traffic on Blue Angel Parkway remained gridlocked until 9 p.m. following a 4 p.m. show conclusion. Drivers reported wait times exceeding two hours just to exit base parking lots. The Escambia County Sheriff's Office deployed 45 deputies for traffic control, up from 30 the previous year.

"You sit there with your engine off watching the sun go down," said Patricia Mullins of Gulf Breeze, a regular attendee since 2018. "The kids are tired, everyone's sunburned, and you're just not moving. We love the show. The leaving part, not so much."

Remote parking and shuttles could theoretically reduce that congestion by distributing the exit load across multiple sites. But only if enough people use them. And only if the shuttle system has capacity to clear thousands of passengers in a reasonable window.

The 2024 plan called for 12 buses running continuous loops. Transit consultants estimated that configuration could move approximately 2,400 people per hour. At that rate, clearing a remote lot of 10,000 visitors would take more than four hours.

The military's constraints

NAS Pensacola operates under security requirements that complicate civilian solutions. Every vehicle entering the installation passes through an access control point. Credentials are checked. Trunks can be inspected. The bottleneck is by design.

Shuttles from a remote lot would still have to clear that checkpoint, though buses can be pre-screened and processed faster than individual vehicles. The Navy has used shuttle access in previous years for VIP guests and sponsors without significant delays.

Expanding that model to general admission is theoretically possible. Practically, it requires coordination between military police, civilian contractors, the city's transit authority, and private shuttle operators. Each entity has its own insurance requirements, scheduling constraints, and chain of command.

"We've done large-scale events before," Dominguez said. "Fleet Week, the centennial celebration, multiple homecomings. We know how to move people. The question is always resources and partnerships."

The runway construction adds another variable. Heavy equipment must be secured or removed from work zones before the public arrives. Contractor crews will lose two full work days, possibly more. The project timeline, already extended once due to supply chain delays, cannot absorb much additional slippage.

NAS Pensacola commanding officer Capt. Terrence Williams addressed the construction issue at an April community briefing.

"The runway project is essential to our long-term mission capability," Williams said. "Homecoming is essential to our community relationship. We are committed to both."

Sixty days to decide

The next planning meeting is scheduled for May 19 at the Pensacola Bay Center. City officials, Navy representatives, the Downtown Improvement Board, Visit Pensacola, and Escambia County administrators are expected to attend. The agenda includes shuttle routing options, parking site evaluations, and cost-sharing proposals.

Hughes said she expects a final framework to be in place by mid-June, leaving three weeks for logistics and public communication before the event.

"That's tight," she acknowledged. "But everyone in that room wants this to work. The alternative is 150,000 people figuring it out on their own, and that's not a plan. That's a traffic jam."

The paint crews will keep working their way down Blue Angel Parkway. The fence will be ready on time. The rest remains to be seen.
